Michelle MacLaren has been replaced as the director of the upcoming "Wonder Woman" film due to creative differences with Warner Bros. Despite this change, the movie starring Gal Gadot remains scheduled for release on June 23, 2017. Warner Bros. is now searching for a new director to helm the project, which marks the first theatrical film centered on the popular female superhero.

More than 35 years after Etan Patz disappeared, a New York jury is deliberating the case against Pedro Hernandez, who confessed to killing the six-year-old but whose defense argues he was mentally incompetent. While Hernandez’s confession has been ruled admissible by a judge, his attorneys maintain that his severe mental illness and borderline IQ prevent him from understanding his actions. Meanwhile, the Patz family continues to seek justice, having previously won a civil judgment against another suspect, Jose Antonio Ramos, though no criminal charges were ever filed against him.

ABC is currently filming a proof of concept for a potential revival of "The Muppets," with "The Big Bang Theory" co-creator Bill Prady and Bob Kushell writing the script for a pilot presentation. If successful, the project could move directly to series, featuring original Muppet performers and a plot centered on the characters attempting to launch a new show despite interpersonal drama. This marks Prady’s second attempt to revive the franchise, leveraging his early career experience with the Henson company after previous interest from Netflix and CBS did not materialize.

A personal account of childhood harassment on Mumbai trains highlights the pervasive nature of sexual violence against women in India, which includes everything from groping to stalking and unwanted attention. Despite studies showing that 80% of women in Mumbai have experienced street harassment, most victims remain silent and rarely report these incidents to authorities. The article argues that this widespread normalization of harassment forces women to restrict their daily activities, urging a societal shift where women are empowered to speak out and confront these behaviors.

Canadian actor Jonathan Crombie, best known for his role as Gilbert Blythe in the beloved "Anne of Green Gables" television movies, has died at the age of 48 due to complications from a brain hemorrhage. Producer Kevin Sullivan remembered Crombie as a dedicated actor who brought significant chemistry and heart to the iconic series, which became a cultural touchstone in Canada and internationally. While Crombie appeared in other productions, he remained deeply proud of his portrayal of Gilbert Blythe, a role that earned him a lasting legacy and affection from fans worldwide.

The recent attack on Garissa University College, which killed 147 people, marks Al-Shabaab's deadliest assault in Kenya and highlights the group's strategic shift toward targeting "soft" civilian sites rather than military bases. This shift is attributed to the group's significant weakening in Somalia due to sustained pressure from African Union forces and U.S. drone and special operations campaigns that have decimated their leadership and territorial control. Consequently, the attack serves as a desperate attempt by an unraveling organization to maintain relevance despite its declining capabilities.

Former rap mogul Marion "Suge" Knight has been ordered to stand trial for murder, attempted murder, and hit-and-run charges following a deadly incident on the set of "Straight Outta Compton." During the preliminary hearing, Judge Ronald Coen lowered Knight's bail to $10 million and dismissed one of the hit-and-run counts, citing legal restrictions on multiple charges involving the same vehicle. Knight faces up to life in prison if convicted, while the sole surviving victim, Cle Sloan, has refused to testify against him despite prosecutors offering immunity.

During National Park Week, which runs from April 18 through April 26, 128 U.S. national parks that typically charge an entrance fee will offer free admission on Saturday and Sunday. The National Park Service and National Park Foundation are hosting various events, including astronomy parties and Junior Ranger activities, to encourage public exploration. Visitors are invited to discover nearby parks via FindYourPark.com and share their experiences using the hashtag #FindYourPark.

A recent CNN report highlights the severe affordable housing crisis in Silicon Valley, where employed families are forced to live in garages, shelters, or overcrowded homes due to high costs. This local struggle reflects a national issue, with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development estimating that 7.7 million low-income households spend more than half their income on rent or live in substandard conditions. In response, HUD is implementing initiatives to preserve existing affordable housing and attract private investment to repair public housing, while urging Congress to remove restrictions on these programs to ensure broader community access.

Debra Lobo, an American citizen and vice principal at a medical school in Karachi, Pakistan, was shot in the head and arm by two assailants on a motorcycle while driving home. The attackers threw pamphlets into her car containing anti-American messages, and she is currently in critical but stable condition at a local hospital. U.S. and Pakistani authorities are actively investigating the incident, which occurred as Lobo was picking up her daughters from school.

A jury of Rolling Stone’s media peers has condemned the magazine’s discredited story about a University of Virginia rape as journalistic malpractice, citing severe lapses in reporting and editing. The investigation revealed that the magazine failed to verify key facts, ignored red flags from the source, and refused to give the accused fraternity a chance to respond before publication. While the magazine’s initial errors are viewed as regrettable, its decision to avoid restructuring its newsroom or holding anyone accountable is criticized as unacceptable.

Jon Cryer reprised his iconic record-store dance from the 1986 film *Pretty in Pink* during a recent episode of CBS's "Late Late Show." He performed the routine alongside host James Corden, who expressed his excitement about fulfilling a childhood dream by recreating the scene. The segment highlighted the enduring appeal of the classic moment, resonating with fans who have grown up alongside the film's legacy.

Governors of Arkansas and Indiana were caught off-guard by the intense public and business backlash against recently passed "religious freedom" bills, which they underestimated despite widespread public opposition. Major corporations, including Marriott, Apple, and Walmart, threatened boycotts and reversed policies to protect their bottom lines, recognizing that supporting discrimination harms their brand loyalty, particularly among younger consumers and the lucrative LGBT travel market. This shift highlights a growing reality where business interests are increasingly prioritizing inclusivity over alliances with socially conservative evangelical groups.

Photographer Ines Dumig created the photo series "Apart Together" to highlight the resilience and humanity of Sahra, a Somali refugee who fled her home at age 14. The project aims to universalize Sahra's story, emphasizing that despite physical separation and bureaucratic dehumanization, shared human emotions connect people across different backgrounds. Through this work, Dumig seeks to restore individual dignity to refugees, portraying them as complex individuals rather than mere statistics.

L.A. Kings hockey player Jarret Stoll was arrested in Las Vegas on charges of possessing cocaine and ecstasy, leading the team to launch an internal investigation. Stoll, 32, was released on $5,000 bail late Friday, while the Kings expressed concern and withheld further comment as they gather facts. The incident involves a player who has been with the team since 2008 and is reportedly dating TV personality Erin Andrews.

After shoplifting a rifle and ammunition from a Walmart in Marana, Arizona, Mario Valencia fled in a stolen car and engaged in a dangerous standoff with police, during which he fired a shot into the air. A police officer ultimately ended the incident by deliberately ramming Valencia’s vehicle with a patrol car, an action that has sparked nationwide debate regarding the justification of such tactics. Valencia was hospitalized and subsequently jailed, facing 15 charges including shoplifting, while police confirmed that although the gun was locked, the security cable was improperly installed, allowing it to be fired.

Two Delaware boys remain in a coma and their father is paralyzed two weeks after their family fell ill while staying at a villa in the U.S. Virgin Islands, with federal officials suspecting pesticide exposure. The EPA has detected methyl bromide, a restricted and highly toxic chemical, in the rented unit, linking the family's severe health issues to a recent fumigation. While the mother has been released, the ongoing investigation focuses on whether environmental regulations were violated during the pest control process.

ISIS claimed responsibility for a suicide car bomb attack near the U.S. Consulate in Irbil, Iraq, which resulted in at least four deaths and 18 injuries. All U.S. Consulate personnel were reported safe, and the vehicle detonated before reaching the building, though the blast caused significant damage to nearby establishments. The U.S. State Department praised the Kurdish government's response and pledged continued cooperation in combating terrorist acts.

South African authorities have arrested more than 300 suspects following deadly xenophobic attacks in Durban that have forced thousands of foreigners to flee their homes. While the government has condemned the violence and praised police efforts to restore order, the unrest stems from local residents accusing immigrants of stealing jobs. President Jacob Zuma has visited displaced individuals to express support, emphasizing that such aggression contradicts South Africa's own history of seeking refuge in neighboring African countries.

Davion Navar Henry, a teenager who went viral in 2013 after pleading for adoption at a Florida church, has finally been adopted by his social worker, Connie Going. After experiencing multiple failed placements and returning to foster care, Henry’s persistent desire for a permanent home convinced Going to adopt him despite her existing three children. The official adoption is scheduled for April 22, marking the end of Henry's years in the foster care system.

Despite Democratic candidates like Elizabeth Warren and Martin O'Malley campaigning on breaking up big banks and addressing economic inequality, the party's reliance on Wall Street donations creates a significant conflict of interest. This financial dependency, exemplified by leaders like Chuck Schumer and past presidents like Barack Obama, undermines the party's ability to enact populist reforms because they must court powerful financial donors to fund their campaigns. Consequently, the current campaign finance system pressures Democrats to prioritize big business interests over their traditional base, making genuine economic reform difficult to achieve.

Three weeks into Saudi Arabia’s airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen, the conflict shows no signs of easing, with civilian casualties mounting and thousands fleeing across the Red Sea. As the death toll rises, fears are growing that the violence is part of a broader proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran for regional dominance. Meanwhile, the UN Security Council has approved an arms embargo and sanctions against the Houthis, aiming to curb the violence and limit the spread of terrorism.

Joy Womack, an American principal ballerina at the Kremlin Ballet Theatre, earns approximately $240 a month, a figure significantly reduced by the weakening Russian ruble and economic sanctions. Despite these financial hardships and a controversial past involving allegations of bribery at the Bolshoi Ballet, Womack prioritizes her artistic experience over financial stability. The theatre maintains that her salary is consistent with her role and local exchange rates, asserting that she is treated equally to her Russian counterparts.

Six young men from Minnesota were arrested for conspiring to join ISIS, with prosecutors describing them as focused individuals engaged in peer-to-peer recruiting rather than being easily influenced. The group plotted for ten months, continuing their efforts even after some associates were caught, and utilized a cooperating witness who had previously recorded their meetings. Four of the suspects appeared in federal court in Minneapolis and were held without bail, while two others were apprehended in San Diego after attempting to cross into Mexico.

Dr. Sanjay Gupta has released a series of CNN documentaries to address the growing medical marijuana revolution and answer public questions regarding its benefits and risks. He highlights potential treatments for conditions such as PTSD, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain, while also acknowledging legitimate concerns about long-term effects on the developing brain. Gupta argues that decades of misinformation have created unnecessary stigma, urging a shift toward evidence-based understanding rather than fear.

After witnessing the poverty and child labor in post-war Nepal, Maggie Doyne used her savings to purchase land and establish the Kopila Valley Children's Home and School. Today, the organization supports approximately 50 children in a communal living environment while educating over 350 students through its BlinkNow Foundation. Doyne continues to live in Nepal year-round, managing the facility with a dedicated staff and a strict protocol to ensure children only enter care when absolutely necessary.

In July, Sierra Sharry and Lane Smith were expecting a baby. Sharry was eight months pregnant when Smith fell and hit his head. He was taken to a hospital in Oklahoma City, but he never recovered. Sharry said on Facebook that July 13, 2014, was the worst day of her life because she lost her best friend and the father of her unborn child. Their son, Taos, was born a few weeks later. When it was time for his six-month photos, Sharry asked the photographer to help make the family look complete in just one picture.

People have different opinions about Indiana’s new religious freedom law. Some people are angry, saying the law allows businesses to discriminate against gay and lesbian people by hiding behind religion. Others, like Indiana Governor Mike Pence, are surprised by the anger. He argues that the law is basically the same as laws already in place in Washington, D.C., and 19 other states. The debate is intense because people disagree on what the law means and what its true purpose is.

Some fans of Lucille Ball want a statue of her removed from a park in her hometown, Celoron, New York. They say the statue looks ugly and does not look like the famous actress from "I Love Lucy." The life-size bronze statue has been compared to singer Conway Twitty, the snake from the movie "Beetlejuice," and actor Steve Buscemi. Even the mayor, Scott Schrecengost, says he does not like the statue, which shows Lucille Ball holding a bottle of a fake drink called Vitameatavegamin. However, the statue has been a popular spot for tourists since 2009. People who visit her birthplace like to take pictures with it.

Muhammadu Buhari became Nigeria’s leader by winning an election, not by force like he did last time. This election was one of the most competitive in the country’s history for five key reasons. First, it was the first time in Nigeria’s history that the opposition party beat the party in power through a fair vote. Buhari, who is 72 years old, won the presidency by getting about two million more votes than the current president, Goodluck Jonathan. This event is very important because Nigeria is Africa’s largest country by population and economy, and it is one of the continent’s biggest oil producers. Nigeria also sends a lot of crude oil to the United States.

People around the world and in Iran were extremely happy, as if Iran had just won the World Cup. But this event is even more important. Young Iranians celebrated by waving flags from their car sunroofs, playing loud music, and talking online using the hashtag #IranTalks. This excitement happened because Iran reached a major agreement with the United States and other countries about its nuclear program. This deal is expected to end Iran’s isolation and remove harsh economic penalties that have been in place for years. Just before midnight on Thursday, Vali Asr Street, a main road in Tehran, became like a street party. Drivers honked their horns, men danced in the middle of the street, and some people showed off U.S. dollar bills.

A fourth man, Dilkhayot Kasimov, has been charged in connection with a plot to help terrorists and for some of the men to join ISIS. This information comes from a court document released on Monday by a federal court in Brooklyn.

Kasimov was added to an updated legal document that also charges three men who were previously arrested: Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, Akhror Saidakhmetov, and Abror Habibov. These three men are accused of two counts of providing support to a foreign terrorist organization, and they have pleaded not guilty. It is not yet clear whether Kasimov has been arrested.

The third "blood moon" in a series of four was the shortest eclipse, but it was still a nice sight for early risers in North America. The moon moved completely into Earth's shadow at 4:58 a.m. Pacific Time (7:58 a.m. Eastern Time) on Saturday. This started a total lunar eclipse that lasted nearly five minutes. NASA says this will be the shortest total eclipse of the century. Before, during, and after the eclipse, the moon looked burnt-orange, which is why total eclipses are called "blood moons."

Istanbul, Turkey (CNN) – Turks were worried on Tuesday. "What is happening? Why can’t I enter the subway?" asked an older woman wearing a white headscarf and carrying shopping bags. She was standing outside a closed entrance to one of Istanbul’s busiest subway stations. She was just one of millions of people in Turkey who were confused and worried because the country suffered its worst power outage in over ten years. For several hours on Tuesday, dozens of cities lost electricity. Millions of people were affected, including passengers stuck in trains and subways that stopped working.

During Holy Week, we should remember what the Bible says about fair pay. Isaiah 58:6 describes a true fast as breaking injustice, stopping workplace exploitation, freeing the oppressed, and canceling debts.

McDonald’s decision to raise wages for 90,000 employees is a big win for fast-food workers and their supporters. By standing together, these workers are making it harder for profitable companies like McDonald’s to pay such low wages that keep workers in poverty.

California is facing a severe drought, and Governor Jerry Brown has ordered mandatory water cuts for residents, businesses, and farms. This is the first time such restrictions have been imposed. Cities and towns must reduce their water usage by 25% over the next nine months. This reduction equals about 1.5 million acre-feet of water (one acre-foot is roughly 325,000 gallons). Governor Brown stated that the era of watering lawns daily is over, signaling a major change in how water is used in the state.

People in the UK are running out of time to decide who to vote for, as voting stations are getting ready to open across the country. This election could change how the government works. The campaign was very short, especially compared to the United States, where candidates often spend years preparing their messages.

The result might give power to the Labour Party, led by Ed Miliband, taking it away from David Cameron’s Conservative government. Or, it could lead to a lot of difficult negotiations as party leaders try to make deals with smaller parties. However, we won’t know the outcome until the polls close late Thursday evening, local time.

This is the time of year when Christians around the world—more than 2 billion people—think about the death and resurrection of Jesus. Because Christian college students were killed in Kenya on Thursday, and Christians in other countries still face danger, we are asking Christians this Holy Week to also remember those who have suffered. Many Christians, as well as other people, have been crucified, beheaded, stoned, enslaved, sexually abused, trafficked, harassed, bombed, or forced to leave their homes. These attacks happen simply because of their faith, which makes them targets for religious extremists.

The Washington Post obtained racist and offensive emails from three Ferguson, Missouri, city employees, who have since resigned or been fired. These messages, sent between the city’s top court clerk and two police officers, were found during a U.S. Justice Department investigation into racial bias in the local police and court system. The emails contain offensive comments about President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, Muslims, and minorities. The Washington Post received the emails on Thursday after requesting them through public records laws, and CNN reviewed them on Friday. The emails involve Police Captain Rick Henke and Sergeant [name cut off].

Two people, including a licensed greyhound trainer, were arrested in Australia after police found at least 55 dead dogs dumped in the Queensland bush. According to Australian media, a 71-year-old man and a 64-year-old woman from Bundaberg were each charged with illegally possessing a firearm. The woman was also charged with obstructing police. Michael Beatty, a spokesman for RSPCA Queensland, said that the investigation is still ongoing. The animal rights group is helping Queensland police with their inquiry.

Two years ago, Mike Premeau and Kathy Danke started a small business called Memories Gourmet Pizza Co. in their town in Wisconsin. They were successful, getting their frozen pizzas—including breakfast and gluten-free options—into stores in Nichols, near Green Bay. They also built a loyal customer base.

However, this week, their business was threatened because people confused them with a different company, Memories Pizza of Walkerton, Indiana. That other business made national news after its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding. As a result, angry people left comments on Memories Gourmet Pizza’s Facebook page and called their phone number to protest.

Archaeologists from the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna found a complete camel skeleton under a cellar in Tulln, Austria, between 2006 and 2007. The site was being prepared for a new shopping center. Experts believe this camel was used by Ottoman soldiers who tried to capture Vienna in the 17th century. At first, researchers thought the bones belonged to a large horse or cow. However, Alfred Galik, an archaeozoologist, identified the animal as a camel by looking at its neck bones, lower jaw, and hand bones.

Andrew Getty, 47, the grandson of J. Paul Getty, died on Tuesday afternoon at his home in Los Angeles. His parents, Ann and Gordon Getty, released a statement confirming the death and asking the media and public to respect the family’s privacy during this difficult time.

The Los Angeles County coroner’s office said the death appears to be due to natural causes or an accident. Investigators found some medication at Getty’s home, but they do not know if he was taking it or what his medical history was.

We may never fully understand why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps on March 24, killing everyone on the plane. A new report shows that he intentionally made the plane descend faster. This is horrifying. As the investigation continues, we will learn more about how much Lubitz hid his mental illness and how much help he asked for. We need to know how his depression affected his ability to fly. Should he have quit his job? Should his doctors have raised concerns? His case highlights important issues about people with mental illness and the shame they often feel.

Taylor is a 23-year-old man who was a convicted murderer but had escaped from jail before being arrested in Chicago overnight.

Police in Illinois had been searching for Taylor since early Wednesday. On that day, he jumped a correctional officer at the Jerome Combs Detention Center in Kankakee. He then fled wearing the guard’s uniform and driving the guard’s SUV.

As his military career comes to an end, Britain’s Prince Harry is going to Australia. The 30-year-old prince arrives on Monday for a four-week visit with the Australian armed forces. According to the Australian Defence Forces, Harry will work and live with Australian Army soldiers in several units in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth. A spokesman said Harry has already spent time with Australian troops several times during his 10 years in the military.

According to the Florida Attorney General’s office, two current Florida prison guards and one former guard trainee have been charged with plotting to kill a former inmate who was about to be released. The men are Thomas Jordan Driver, 25; David Elliot Moran, 47; and Charles Thomas Newcomb, 42.

An FBI informant met them after going undercover in a branch of the Ku Klux Klan called the Traditional American Knights of the Ku Klux Klan. Court documents state that Driver told the informant he had fought with the inmate and that he and Moran wanted the inmate dead.

On Thursday in Lausanne, Switzerland, a group of world powers called the P5+1 finished a long and complicated series of talks with Iran. They reached a basic agreement on Iran’s nuclear program. It is not yet clear if this agreement will work. The two sides have until the end of June to finalize the details and write the plan down. Even so, these talks were historic, especially because relations between the United States and Iran had been frozen for a long time. The negotiations were not glamorous. Instead, they showed what diplomacy can look like when it is both very good and very chaotic.

On Monday morning, an improvised bomb exploded near a United Nations vehicle in Garowe, a city in northeastern Somalia. The attack killed six people, including four aid workers from UNICEF, the international children’s agency. Somalia’s President called the bombing "an attack against the future of our country."

The United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia said the explosion happened around 8 a.m. in Garowe, which is the administrative capital of the Puntland region. The terrorist group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the attack. This incident follows a separate event on Sunday, when three African Union troops were killed in an ambush in Somalia’s Lower Shabelle region.

Prince Harry arrived in Australia on Monday to spend four weeks working with the country’s military. Before starting his duties, the 30-year-old visited the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, the capital city. He paid his respects at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier.

A crowd gathered outside the memorial. Some people took photos of the prince, and one boy held up a sign that said, "Red Heads Rule!" to celebrate Harry’s red hair.

According to the Australian Defence Forces, Harry will live and work alongside soldiers in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth during his stay.

Australia, a key ally of the United States, has agreed to share some intelligence with Iran. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop described the deal as an "informal arrangement" focused on tracking Australians who travel to Iraq to fight for ISIS. However, one Australian lawmaker criticized the move, calling it "dancing with the devil."

Over the weekend, Bishop became the first Australian government minister to visit Iran in 12 years, where she met with President Hassan Rouhani. The intelligence-sharing deal was announced in an interview released on Monday, which Bishop gave to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation while she was in Tehran.

Tests on the flight data recorder, also known as the "black box," from Germanwings Flight 9525 show that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz intentionally made the plane go down faster. This information comes from the French air accident investigation agency, the BEA.

Recovery teams found the black box on Thursday. They had been searching the mountainside in the French Alps for several days since the plane crashed on March 24. The BEA stated that its teams started looking at the data from the recorder immediately.

A 110-day chase of a suspected poaching ship, which traveled from the Antarctic to the coast of West Africa, ended in an unusual way. Conservationists from the group Sea Shepherd were following the ship, named the *Thunder*, when they rescued its crew. The *Thunder* is the subject of an Interpol "purple notice" for suspected fraud and fisheries crimes. The chase began months ago in the Southern Ocean when Sea Shepherd’s ship, the *Bob Barker*, spotted the *Thunder*. The pursuit ended early Monday in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of West Africa, when the *Bob Barker* received a distress call from the *Thunder*.

Most days, 16-year-old Jason Zobott goes to Huntley High School in suburban Chicago at 7:30 a.m., just like other high school students. However, what he does after that is unusual. Jason is part of a blended learning program at his school. This program combines online lessons with traditional classroom teaching. One-third of the school’s 2,700 students are in this program. By 2015, the school hopes to enroll most of its students in it. Jason, who is a top student and balances schoolwork with many extracurricular activities, says, “Having to work online makes it really accessible to do the work that I have to get done. I can learn on my own.”

Days after a deadly Al-Shabaab attack in Garissa, Kenya, launched airstrikes against the terrorist group in Somalia. A military source confirmed the strikes but said they were not revenge for the massacre at Garissa University College, which killed nearly 150 people last week. The source explained that these attacks are part of ongoing military operations that began in 2011, not a response to the recent tragedy. As is common practice, the source did not give their name to the media.

Pope Francis used his traditional Easter speech to remind the world that the Vatican is a country and that he acts as a moral leader. He spoke about the pain people are facing in current wars and asked for an end to violence everywhere. He specifically called for the fighting to stop in Iraq and Syria and for help to reach those who need it. He urged the international community not to ignore the huge humanitarian crisis and the suffering of many refugees.

Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh, a 29-year-old U.S. citizen with alleged ties to al Qaeda, did not enter a plea during his first court appearance on Thursday. He faces charges for allegedly conspiring to provide material support to terrorists. Al Farekh was deported from Pakistan to the United States. According to a legal complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Brooklyn, he is accused of plotting to fight against American forces abroad. CNN counterterrorism analyst Philip Mudd called the news "something to celebrate."

Saudi Arabia reported its first known military death since it started airstrikes in Yemen. According to the state-run Saudi Press Agency, a Saudi border guard named Cpl. Salman Ali Yahya al-Maliki was killed during a gunfight with militants on Wednesday night. The shooting happened in the Asir region of southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the border. Militants in the mountains of Yemen fired at Saudi border troops, who then fired back. In addition to the guard who died, 10 other people were injured, but their injuries were not life-threatening.

I was a little nervous when I went to the Al Marmoum camel race in Dubai. Because I am the only person from a Gulf country on the CNN team, people expected me to know about camel racing, which is a very old tradition in this area. Even though I tried to wear a kandora, which is traditional clothing in the UAE, I still felt like an outsider because my way of thinking is modern.

A friendly farm owner took us into the majlis, which is a meeting place. The camel owners were gathering there. The large room looked like a fancy theater. The owners sat on the floor eating a'aish, a traditional Arabic dish made of fish and rice. Everyone was talking loudly and excitedly.

Havana, Cuba (CNN) – Charlie Hill sits in a dark bar on a bright, sunny day in Havana. He says, "Hey man," in a rough voice and gives a nod, showing he knows you have been looking for him. Many people have been looking for Charlie Hill for a long time. For 43 years, Cuba has protected Hill from being charged with killing a New Mexico police officer and hijacking an airplane to Havana. Hill, now 65, agreed to speak with CNN after we spent two years trying to contact him. He wants to talk about how he is now thinking about leaving his safe place in Cuba and returning to the United States.

Documents obtained by CNN show that when the Missouri National Guard prepared to go to Ferguson, Missouri, to help stop the protests, they used strong military language. They called the protesters "enemy forces" and "adversaries."

The Guard went to Ferguson to support local police. However, many community leaders and civil rights activists accused the police of using too much force and making the tense situation worse. The protests happened sporadically from August until the end of last year.

On Tuesday, gunmen attacked the Somali education ministry in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. This happened after a suicide car bomb exploded at the entrance of the building. The attack killed at least 12 people and injured 16 others.

The militant group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the attack. A spokesman for the group said they were responsible. According to a government security official, two suicide bombers drove cars into the building and set them off. Then, five gunmen went inside and shot people.

Gregory Margolin, now 87, has lived through two wars. As a 16-year-old Jewish soldier, he fought for the Soviet Red Army against the Nazis during World War II. While he was fighting, his family fled. Margolin says he did not reveal that he was Jewish, but it did not matter because people were being killed everywhere around him.

This year, he found himself in Ukraine, once again surrounded by war. Margolin was a sniper who eventually became an army commander. He still wears his old uniform, which is covered with military medals. His granddaughter, Liora, is amazed by his war stories and wonders how he managed to survive.

It has been exactly one year since more than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls were taken from their dorms at night in Chibok, in northeastern Nigeria. They are still missing.

We should feel ashamed that this happened. It is shameful that violent criminals can harm young girls without facing consequences. It is also shameful that people lose interest in such terrible events so quickly.

In Norway, digital technology is replacing FM radio. The country plans to stop using FM radio completely within two years, making it the first nation to do so. This does not mean people will lose access to radio; they will just listen using digital signals instead.

Officials in Oslo say that many Norwegians have already switched. There are only five stations available on FM, but there are four times as many stations on the Digital Audio Broadcasting network. According to Culture Minister Thorhild Widvey, half of Norway’s 5 million people already listen to radio digitally.

Everyone enjoys a good comeback story, especially one involving dinosaurs. A new study suggests that the Brontosaurus should have its own name again. For over 100 years, it was removed from science books.

O.C. Marsh first named the Brontosaurus in 1879. He did this after receiving 25 crates of bones found at Como Bluff in Wyoming, according to the Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History. The dinosaur was similar to, but not as large as, the Apatosaurus, which had been discovered a few years earlier. Marsh called it the "Brontosaurus," which means "thunder lizard."

Al Qaeda has announced a reward in a conflict involving multiple groups in Yemen. The group, known as Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), offered 20 kilograms of gold to anyone who kills or captures two prominent Shia Muslim leaders. These leaders are Houthi rebel leader Abdelmalik Bedrudin Al-Houthi and former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh.

The group posted this offer online in a news release and a wanted poster. The amount of gold is worth about $774,000. AQAP called these two men the "two heads of evil." AQAP is just one of several groups fighting to control Yemen.

Before landing his gyrocopter on the Capitol lawn on Wednesday, Doug Hughes explained his plans and reasons on a website called thedemocracyclub.org. The 61-year-old postal worker from Florida wrote in an online post titled "Your Pilot" that he wanted to highlight corruption in Washington, D.C., and offer solutions to it. He stated that his flight was not a secret. Before taking off, he sent an email to info@barackobama.com. The message was meant to convince Capitol officials that he was not a threat and that shooting him down would cause more problems than letting him deliver letters to Congress.

Rio de Janeiro is facing more problems ahead of the 2016 Olympics after many dead fish were found in the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon. With just over a year left before the city hosts the rowing and canoe events, officials from Rio’s legislative assembly started an investigation on Monday. They are looking into why the fish died in the lagoon and in other lakes and bays across the state where this has happened. The investigation will be done with help from the State Environmental Institute (INEA) and the State Secretariat for the Environment.

Anthony Ray Hinton is 58 years old, but he is just now getting used to the outside world. He spent nearly 30 years on death row in Alabama. Because of this long imprisonment, simple things like using a fork, going out at night, or sleeping without someone watching him feel strange to him.

One week ago, his murder convictions were canceled, and he was released from a county jail in Birmingham. He told CNN’s Brooke Baldwin that he has to pinch himself to believe he is free. He said it will take some time to get used to his freedom.

For most of those 30 years, Hinton lived in a very small cell that was only 5 by 7 feet.

After the UK election debate featuring seven party leaders, the polls showed there was no clear winner. The leaders were David Cameron (Conservatives), Ed Miliband (Labour), Nick Clegg (Liberal Democrats), Nigel Farage (UK Independence Party), Natalie Bennett (Green Party), Nicola Sturgeon (Scottish National Party), and Leanne Wood (Plaid Cymru).

Two different polling groups gave similar results. Comres, which organized the debate for ITV, found that Cameron, Miliband, and Farage tied for first place with 21% each, while Sturgeon was close behind with 20%. A New York judge has ruled that Facebook is a valid way to serve divorce papers. This means a woman in Brooklyn can use the social media site to officially notify her husband about the divorce.

Ellanora Arthur Baidoo has been trying to divorce her husband, Victor Sena Blood-Dzraku, for several years. Her lawyer, Andrew Spinnell, said they could not find him to hand-deliver the legal documents. Court papers show that Baidoo can still call her husband, but he told her he does not have a home address or a job.

This sounds like a science fiction movie. A person has a terrible accident, ends up in the hospital, and is brain dead while on life support. Instead of donating organs to save up to eight people, doctors ask the family to donate the entire body to save just one person. This could help someone who is paralyzed from the neck down but has a healthy mind. Although this idea seems crazy, Italian doctor Sergio Canavero says we are close to making it happen. He calls the project HEAVEN, which stands for Head Anastomosis Venture. "Anastomosis" means surgically connecting two body parts.

Police say Anthony Stokes’ story did not end happily. On Tuesday, the teenager, who had received a heart transplant, stole a car, broke into a house, and shot at an elderly woman. He then led police on a fast car chase and died after crashing into a pole.

In 2013, Stokes’ family told the media that an Atlanta hospital refused to give him a new heart. The hospital said in a letter that they rejected him because he had a history of not following medical advice. At that time, Mark Bell spoke for the Stokes family.

At Garissa University College in Kenya, the sun had not yet risen, and most students were still sleeping in their beds. A few students had woken up early to attend Christian prayers. The attack began around 5:30 a.m. on Thursday (10:30 p.m. ET on Wednesday) with an explosion and gunshots at the front gates. The attackers continued shooting as they moved through the campus. The Red Cross reported that they stopped at a girls' dormitory. According to lecturer Joel Ayora, the attackers also burst into a room where Christians had gathered and took people hostage.

Freddie Gray, 25, was buried at New Shiloh Baptist Church in West Baltimore. A gospel choir sang as a large crowd gathered to honor him. Gray died 15 days ago while in police custody. He was arrested for carrying weapons and died from a serious spinal cord injury. His death caused widespread anger toward the Baltimore Police Department. Gray’s death is the most recent in a series of high-profile cases involving African-Americans and law enforcement. Many people have demanded answers about what happened to Gray. His funeral was attended by civil rights leaders, politicians, and family members of other people who died in police custody.

I have worked as a chef since I was 14, but I didn’t start fighting for food policy until much later. In 2007, I saw a young girl my wife was mentoring looking through the trash for food. This experience inspired me to start Food Policy Action and get involved in political issues about food, such as hunger and factory farms. I haven’t worked alone on this. A major influence was "The Meatrix," a 2003 animated video made by the GRACE Communications Foundation. This video, which parodied the movie "The Matrix," clearly showed the health and environmental dangers of factory farming.

Dan Swangard is a doctor who has seen many patients die. He has watched people pass away in hospitals while receiving pain medication and feeling scared. He has also seen death take weeks or months, with frightened family members standing by without being able to help.

Recently, this topic became personal for him. In 2013, he was diagnosed with a rare type of cancer that had spread. To treat it, surgeons removed parts of his pancreas and liver, as well as his entire spleen and gallbladder. The surgery was successful, but Swangard, who is 48 years old, knows there is a high chance the cancer will come back.

A Saudi source told CNN that Saudi special forces helped Yemeni fighters fight against the Houthis and their allies in Aden. The Saudi soldiers were on the ground but did not fight directly. Instead, they helped plan and guide the battle against Houthi forces and fighters who support former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh. The Saudis also helped drop weapons and communication equipment by parachute.

Meanwhile, Houthi rebels left the presidential palace and other important areas in the southern port city of Aden after heavy airstrikes by Saudi planes. This move was a change from the day before, when the Houthis had taken control of the presidential palace.

A mother from Detroit was charged with murder and torture this week. She was arrested last month after police found the bodies of two of her children in a freezer.

Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy charged Mitchelle Angela Blair with killing her 13-year-old daughter, Stoni Ann Blair, and her 9-year-old son, Stephen Gage Berry.

Detroit Police Chief James Craig said the bodies were found wrapped in plastic inside the freezer on March 24. A bailiff discovered them while carrying out a court-ordered eviction.

A medical examiner determined that Stoni died from multiple blunt force injuries. Stephen died from multiple blunt force injuries and burns.

Wladimir Klitschko, the current world heavyweight boxing champion, has a major title fight coming up, but he is mostly worried about the struggle for democracy in his home country, Ukraine. He spoke to CNN from his training center in Miami before his match with American challenger Bryant Jennings on April 25 in New York. Klitschko said the crisis in Ukraine has left him shocked and upset. He explained that his country is suffering because of the war with Russia. He stressed that Ukraine did not attack Russia; instead, Russia is the one attacking.

Michael Keaton hosted "Saturday Night Live" for the third time this weekend. He made small references to his roles in "Beetlejuice" and "Batman." In his opening speech, he noted that much has changed since he first hosted the show in 1982. He mentioned that he has a 31-year-old son and a 28-year-old girlfriend. Fans who wanted to see him fully act out his famous characters were likely disappointed. Cast members Taran Killam and Bobby Moynihan sang a song asking him to play Batman and Beetlejuice with them. However, Keaton only responded with a few short jokes.

About a month ago, Kamron Taylor was found guilty of murder in an Illinois court. On Wednesday morning, he was in an Illinois jail. He hid outside his cell, waiting to attack. He hit a guard who was checking the cells, took the guard’s uniform and keys, and walked out of the jail. He then got into the guard’s 2012 brown Chevrolet Equinox SUV. No one knows where the 23-year-old is now. He was supposed to be sentenced in May. The SUV was found around 8:30 a.m. (9:30 a.m.

A New York City detective, Ian Cyrus, has been suspended for allegedly stealing $3,000 during an illegal cigarette raid. Police spokesman Stephen Davis confirmed the suspension.

Video from a local news station shows Cyrus putting cash into a bag before leaving the Yemen Deli and Grocery store in Brooklyn last Friday. The detectives had arrested two employees for selling loose cigarettes.

The store’s manager, Ali Abdullah, noticed the money was missing from a box. He initially thought one of his employees had taken it. However, after checking the security cameras, he was shocked by what he saw.

London (CNN) The Hatton Garden heist, which will likely be remembered by this name, was a terrible event for safe deposit box owners but a perfect scenario for a movie. Over the recent holiday weekend, thieves used heavy cutting tools and climbing gear to break into the vault of a well-known safe deposit company in central London that has been operating for 60 years. They may have had up to four days to search through countless safe deposit boxes. Reports say they stole hundreds of thousands of pounds worth of jewelry and cash. One former police official estimates the total value could be as high as 200 million pounds, or about $300 million.

As we get closer to April 27, the day South Africa celebrates the first elections after apartheid in 1994, we are seeing another wave of deadly attacks against African migrants. People are expressing their anger on social media using the hashtag "#WeAreAfrica" to show that we need to stand together against this violence. These repeated attacks on migrants and their belongings suggest that South Africa’s dream is failing. That dream was about a country with many different ethnic groups, where everyone—no matter their race or class—could live with dignity.

In 1989, Ayatollah Khomeini said he was "drinking poison" when he agreed to a ceasefire to end the eight-year war with Iraq. The war had helped define his government, the Islamic Republic, which he had started just one year before Saddam Hussein invaded Iran. Khomeini united the country, including both his supporters and his critics, to fight against the enemy. He kept the war going for eight years, even though Saddam was ready to stop fighting, which helped strengthen the Islamic Republic. By the time the war ended, the economy was ruined, and his most loyal volunteers were gone.

Sustainable development suggests that unchecked capitalism is too powerful and dangerous. The global economy is growing very fast, doubling in size every generation. However, because Earth has limited resources and the population is increasing by one billion people every 15 years, this rapid growth is damaging the natural environment and the social systems that keep life comfortable and fair. Sustainable development provides a solution to this crisis. In reality, unchecked capitalism is driven by greed.

The United States benefits greatly from being a space-faring nation. Space access helps protect U.S. national security, defense, and the economy. To fight current and future conflicts, combat terrorism, and handle global threats, the U.S. military relies on space-based tools like intelligence, GPS, and communications satellites. However, as global threats grow and the need for reliable space access increases, the U.S. faces a serious problem: it depends too much on Russian technology to meet its national security needs.

One year after nearly 300 schoolgirls were kidnapped by Boko Haram in Nigeria, Malala Yousafzai sent them an open letter on Monday. Malala, who won the Nobel Peace Prize at age 17, was also targeted by militants who opposed girls' education. She survived an attack by the Taliban in Pakistan, where she had been writing about the importance of staying in school. In her letter, she urges the Nigerian government and the rest of the world to do more to rescue the girls. This message comes shortly after Nigeria held an election.

On Tuesday evening, South African soldiers were sent to stop deadly violence against immigrants. Their first mission was in Jeppestown, a neighborhood in Johannesburg where the attacks began on Friday. While the soldiers guarded the area, police raided a hostel there. Earlier, Defense Minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula announced that these troops would help police in areas where there are not enough officers to stop the attacks. She said this move does not mean the police are failing.

Iranian state media reported that eight Iranian border guards were killed in fighting with militants near the Pakistan border. The clashes happened on Monday in Negur, a town in southeastern Iran. Iranian forces killed three of the militants during the fight.

According to Ali Asghar Mirshekari, the deputy governor of Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, the militants crossed into Iran from Pakistan. Iranian officials have asked Pakistan to help catch the remaining attackers.

Island travelers, listen up: Providenciales in the Turks and Caicos is now TripAdvisor’s number one island in the world. Last year, it was ranked second. This year, it moved up to first place, taking the top spot from Ambergris Caye in Belize.

Ambergris Caye had been the number one island for two years in a row, but this year it fell out of the top 10 entirely. Why did it drop? A TripAdvisor spokesperson, Julie Cassetina, said it is hard to explain because the winners change every year based on what travelers have to say.

The "Star Wars" story continues to grow. At a fan event in Anaheim, California, on Sunday, the plot for the 2016 movie "Star Wars: Rogue One" was announced. Director Gareth Edwards showed a short preview clip and shared details about the film. Disney calls this type of movie an "anthology" rather than a "spinoff." The movie stars Felicity Jones.

The story happens between "Episode III: Revenge of the Sith" and "Episode IV: A New Hope" (the original 1977 "Star Wars" film). It follows a group of rebels who go on a secret mission to steal the plans for the Death Star. Felicity Jones plays one of these rebel soldiers.

Tehran, Iran (CNN) There is a Persian saying: "A good year is determined by its spring." Many Iranians feel that the recent historic decision by Tehran and six world powers—the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Russia, and China—to keep talking about nuclear issues under a "joint comprehensive plan of action" means this year’s Norouz (the Persian New Year, which began on March 21) will be a great one. Even though some strict political opponents might try to cause trouble and complain that the preliminary agreement isn’t what they wanted, many people see it as excellent progress and are happy with it.

Ferguson, Missouri (CNN) [Update at 11:45 p.m. ET] Two Black men, Ella Jones and Wesley Bell, were elected to the Ferguson City Council on Tuesday. This means that three of the six council members are now Black. [Original story, published at 6:52 p.m. ET] Dark clouds filled the sky, and radio warnings about flash floods crackled through the air. Despite the rain, the city opened its voting places at 6 a.m. for local elections, which usually have very few voters. But this time was different.
